input.title: Rounding a progress percentage in Python
input.page: VS Code with progress.py open. A progress_percent function returns round(done / total * 100), followed by four pytest tests. The terminal shows two failures: (1, 8) gives 12 instead of 13, and (29, 200) gives 14 instead of 15.
input.words: wait why is it 12 tho, 1 over 8 is 12.5, that rounds to 13

expected.pain_point: He assumes Python's round() rounds halves up. Python 3's round() uses round-half-to-even (banker's rounding), so round(12.5) returns 12.

criteria: V1 (visual): Marks the round( token on line 8 (ring, underline or box) as the source of the 12.
V2 (visual): Marks the failing assertion 'assert 12 == 13' in the terminal, or links it to line 8 with an arrow.
S1 (voice): Confirms his arithmetic: 1/8*100 really is 12.5. The surprise is how round() treats halves.
C1 (subject): States correctly that Python 3's round() rounds exact .5 cases to the nearest even integer (banker's rounding), so round(12.5) is 12. It must not blame float imprecision for this case.
R1 (reveal): Does not give the replacement line or the integer formula (200*done + total)//(2*total).
G1 (general): Answers only why it's 12, possibly with a quick check like round(13.5) or round(2.5). It does not jump ahead to the 29/200 issue.

expected.pain_point: He thinks int(x + 0.5) gives correct half-up rounding everywhere. He hasn't noticed that the other failing test (29, 200) will still fail, because the float value is not exactly 14.5.

criteria: V1 (visual): Points to the second failing test (line 20 or 'assert 14 == 15') as the case to check his idea against.
S1 (voice): Acknowledges that int(x + 0.5) would fix the 1-of-8 case.
S2 (voice): Prompts him to test the idea on (29, 200), for example by asking what 29/200*100 actually evaluates to in Python, instead of approving the fix outright.
C1 (subject): Does not claim that int(x + 0.5) is a correct general fix. If it mentions limits, they are accurate (fails on values stored just below .5; also wrong for negatives).
R1 (reveal): Does not give the integer-only formula or the final return line.
G1 (general): Gives one nudge toward discovering the float issue himself, not a full explanation plus the fix.

input.subject: programming
input.title: Rounding a progress percentage in Python
input.page: VS Code with progress.py open. A progress_percent function returns round(done / total * 100), followed by four pytest tests. The terminal shows two failures: (1, 8) gives 12 instead of 13, and (29, 200) gives 14 instead of 15.
input.words: why would that one be different tho, 29 over 200 is literally 14.5

expected.pain_point: He doesn't know that 0.145 has no exact binary float representation. 29/200*100 evaluates to 14.499999999999998, so adding 0.5 and truncating gives 14.
expected.key: Replace line 8 with: return (200 * done + total) // (2 * total). This is exact integer half-up rounding of 100*done/total for non-negative ints. All four tests pass: (7,20)->35, (1,8)->13, (29,200)->15, (0,0)->0 via the guard.

criteria: V1 (visual): Marks the expression done / total * 100 on line 8 as where the value goes wrong.
V2 (visual): Draws a small panel in empty editor space showing the chain: 29/200 → 0.14499999… ; ×100 → 14.499999999999998 ; +0.5 → 14.999… ; int → 14.
S1 (voice): Explains that 0.145 can't be stored exactly in binary floating point, so it is stored slightly below and the product lands just under 14.5.
C1 (subject): The numbers are correct: 29/200*100 is 14.499999999999998 in Python. Adding 0.5 and truncating gives 14. round() also gives 14.
R1 (reveal): Does not yet give the integer-arithmetic fix or the final line.
G1 (general): Ties the explanation to his circled 'assert 14 == 15' and to his +0.5 idea, and may end by suggesting he avoid floats, without giving the method.

input.title: Critiquing a Keynote chart slide: contrast and label size
input.page: A Keynote window with the student's slide 'Volunteer Hours, Q2 vs Q3': a grouped bar chart for four sites drawn in two near-identical pale greens, with pale gray titles and labels on an off-white slide. The Format inspector is open on the Axis tab and shows 9 pt labels in #C8C8C8 and the two series fills.
input.words: ok be honest, is this slide good to go? i'm presenting it tomorrow

expected.pain_point: He wants a yes or no and can't see that the slide will be unreadable when projected. The two series look the same and every label is faint.

criteria: V1 (visual): Marks a bar pair or the legend swatches to show that Q2 and Q3 are nearly indistinguishable.
V2 (visual): Marks the faint axis labels (y or x) or the faint title as hard to read.
S1 (voice): Gives an honest verdict that the slide is not ready yet, because readability will fail when projected.
C1 (subject): Correctly names the problem as low contrast and small text (pale gray labels, nearly identical series colors), not just taste or prettiness.
R1 (reveal): Does not dump a full redesign with exact sizes, hex codes and a rewritten title in this first turn.
G1 (general): Prioritizes one or two biggest issues instead of a long checklist, and ideally invites him to look (for example, can he tell Q2 from Q3 at a glance).

input.subject: presentation design
input.title: Critiquing a Keynote chart slide: contrast and label size
input.page: A Keynote window with the student's slide 'Volunteer Hours, Q2 vs Q3': a grouped bar chart for four sites drawn in two near-identical pale greens, with pale gray titles and labels on an off-white slide. The Format inspector is open on the Axis tab and shows 9 pt labels in #C8C8C8 and the two series fills.
input.words: wait the labels look fine on my laptop tho

expected.pain_point: He is judging legibility from 50 cm away on a bright laptop screen. He doesn't realize that viewing distance and projector washout make 9 pt pale gray text (about 1.6:1 contrast) disappear.

criteria: V1 (visual): Marks the inspector's 9 pt size field and/or the #C8C8C8 label color.
V2 (visual): Marks the axis labels he is asking about.
S1 (voice): Explains why his laptop misleads him: he sits close to a bright screen, while the audience is far away and projectors wash out pale colors.

C1 (subject): Any numbers given are right: pale gray on near-white is roughly 1.6:1 against a 4.5:1 guideline, and 9 pt is far too small for projection (about 18 to 24 pt or more is typical). Makes no false claims.
R1 (reveal): Does not redesign the whole slide or write his new title. Stays on the labels.
G1 (general): Directly addresses his 'looks fine to me' doubt with the reason, rather than just repeating that the labels are bad.

input.subject: presentation design
input.title: Critiquing a Keynote chart slide: contrast and label size
input.page: A Keynote window with the student's slide 'Volunteer Hours, Q2 vs Q3': a grouped bar chart for four sites drawn in two near-identical pale greens, with pale gray titles and labels on an off-white slide. The Format inspector is open on the Axis tab and shows 9 pt labels in #C8C8C8 and the two series fills.
input.words: ok can you just tell me what colors to make the bars

expected.pain_point: He wants a palette, but he hasn't decided what the chart's message is (Millbrook's Q3 jump). Color should make the story series dark and the other one muted. The two must differ in lightness, not only in hue.
expected.key: Not ready. The chart is illegible when projected. The Q2 and Q3 fills (#CFE8E4 vs #C4E6D6) are almost the same. The labels are 9 pt #C8C8C8 on #FBFBF7 (about 1.6:1 contrast). The title is faint and says nothing about the takeaway. Fixes: darken all text to at least 4.5:1 (for example #333 to #444). Raise the axis labels to about 18 to 24 pt and the title to 36 pt or more. Make the story series (Q3) a dark saturated color and push Q2 to light gray. Label the series directly or enlarge the legend. Replace the title with the takeaway: Millbrook's hours nearly doubled (290 to 530) while the other sites stayed flat or fell.

criteria: V1 (visual): Marks the two nearly identical series fills in the inspector.
V2 (visual): Marks a bar pair (ideally Millbrook) to anchor the question of which series carries the story.
S1 (voice): Asks him which comparison or quarter is the point of the slide before settling on colors.
S2 (voice): States the principle: make the story series dark and saturated and mute the other one (for example light gray).
C1 (subject): Says the two series must differ in lightness, not just hue, so the difference survives projection, grayscale and color blindness.
R1 (reveal): Does not state the takeaway for him (Millbrook nearly doubled / +83%) and does not write his headline.
G1 (general): Takes one step: decide the message, then the colors. Does not just hand over hex codes without that link.

input.title: Checking a Step Bracket Drawing for Missing and Redundant Dimensions
input.page: A Preview PDF of a dimensioning check. A 6061 aluminum step bracket is shown in third-angle top and front views, with an isometric reference view and a title block. Q3 says one feature is not fully located and one group of dimensions over-constrains the part.
input.words: wait how is the 60 a problem, it literally adds up, 30 plus 60 is 90

expected.pain_point: He thinks over-dimensioning only means numbers that contradict each other. He doesn't see that every dimension carries a tolerance, so a closed chain (30 + 60 = 90) gives the machinist conflicting limits even when the nominal values agree.

criteria: V1 (visual): Marks the three chained dimensions (30, 60, 90) together as one loop, for example by ringing or boxing all three or bracketing the chain.
V2 (visual): Draws a small panel in empty space showing the tolerance stack, e.g. '30±0.2 + 60±0.2 → 89.6 to 90.4' against '90±0.2 → 89.8 to 90.2'.
S1 (voice): Says that matching numbers aren't the issue. Each dimension has a tolerance, and the loop gives the machinist two conflicting controls on the same length.
R1 (reveal): Does not say which of the three dimensions to remove, and does not mention the hole's missing location.
C1 (subject): Correctly defines over-dimensioning as a redundant or closed dimension chain, not as an arithmetic error.
G1 (general): Answers his 'how is it a problem if it adds up' directly and briefly, then stops so he can decide what to do.

input.subject: engineering drawing
input.title: Checking a Step Bracket Drawing for Missing and Redundant Dimensions

input.words: ok ok so just tell me which one i cross out, the 30, the 60 or the 90

expected.pain_point: He wants a rule handed to him. He doesn't realize that removing any one link breaks the loop, and that the choice is about which sizes matter functionally. The overall length and the upright width are design sizes, so the leftover segment becomes the derived one, deleted or shown as a reference.

criteria: S1 (voice): Explains that removing any one of the three breaks the loop, and that you choose by keeping the sizes that matter for function or fit.
S2 (voice): Asks him a guiding question, such as which length the design really cares about and which one is just whatever is left over.

V1 (visual): Puts a mark (underline or ring) on the overall 90 and the upright width 30 as the 'keep for function' candidates, or uses arrows to show which features they control (the overall length and the upright).
R1 (reveal): Does not flatly say 'cross out the 60' or slash the 60 before he picks. Mentioning that the removed one can be kept as a reference in parentheses is fine.
C1 (subject): Anything said about drawing conventions is correct, e.g. overall dimensions are usually kept and a redundant one may appear in parentheses as reference.
G1 (general): Responds to his push for the answer by giving a decision rule he can apply in one step, not a lecture.

expected.pain_point: He assumes the hole is located because it has one location dimension. A hole center in the top view needs two coordinates (left-right and front-back), and only the left-right one (65) is given. The front-back location is missing.

Add a dimension in the top view from the front edge to the hole center: 20 (the hole is centered in the 40 depth).

V2 (visual): Ties the existing 65 to the left-right direction only, e.g. by underlining it and labeling it 'x'.
S1 (voice): Says a hole center in the plan view needs two location dimensions, and asks him to check whether both directions are given.
R1 (reveal): Does not state that the front-back location is missing, does not give the value 20, and does not draw the missing dimension.
C1 (subject): Correctly says that Ø12 THRU fully gives size and depth (through), so only location is in question, and that 40 and the other dimensions are complete.

input.subject: music theory
input.title: Counting Dotted Notes and Ties Across a Bar Line in a 3/4 Chorale
input.page: A Preview PDF of a worksheet with a four-measure SATB chorale excerpt in F major, 3/4, on a grand staff. Three questions ask where notes begin and how long tied notes last in measures 2 and 3.
input.words: ok wait what does the dot do here, is this like two beats now?

expected.pain_point: He doesn't know that a dot adds half of the note's own value. So he can't tell that the dotted quarter lasts 1½ beats and that the eighth after it starts on the '&' of 2.

criteria: V1 (visual): Rings or points at the soprano dotted quarter in m. 2, specifically its augmentation dot.

V2 (visual): Draws a small panel in empty space showing the dot rule as arithmetic: quarter = 1 beat, dot adds half of that, 1 + ½ = 1½. It must not write out the full count sequence for the soprano line.
S1 (voice): Says the dot adds half of the note's own value, so it is not two beats. A dotted quarter is one and a half beats.
C1 (subject): Everything stated about duration is correct: in 3/4 a quarter = 1 beat and a dotted quarter = 1½ beats, not 2. It does not confuse the dot with a tie or a fermata.
R1 (reveal): Does not say, write or draw where the B-flat 4 eighth begins ('& of 2'). Does not give the finished counts for Q1.
G1 (general): Answers his actual question about the dot, then hands him one next step, such as counting '1 & 2' over the held note to find where the next note starts. It does not go on to Q2 or Q3.

input.subject: music theory
input.title: Counting Dotted Notes and Ties Across a Bar Line in a 3/4 Chorale
input.page: A Preview PDF of a worksheet with a four-measure SATB chorale excerpt in F major, 3/4, on a grand staff. Three questions ask where notes begin and how long tied notes last in measures 2 and 3.
input.words: ok got that one. now this curvy thing going over the bar line, is that like one note or two? just tell me how many beats it is lol

expected.pain_point: He doesn't know that a tie joins two same-pitch notes into one held sound, so their values add. He also hasn't noticed that the second note, in m. 3, is dotted, so the sum crosses the bar line as 1 + 1½.

criteria: V1 (visual): Marks the tie itself, for example by tracing or underlining the curve, or by drawing an arrow along it from the m. 2 note to the m. 3 note.
V2 (visual): Marks the two tied noteheads separately so he sees there are two values to add, for example rings or '?' labels on each. Bonus if the dot on the m. 3 note is pointed out.
S1 (voice): Explains that a tie means one sound: the pitch is sung once and held for both notes' values added together, even across the bar line.
S2 (voice): Asks him what each of the two notes is worth, and cues him to notice that the second one has a dot.
R1 (reveal): Does not state the total (2½ / two and a half beats) despite his request.
C1 (subject): Correct theory: a tie joins notes of the same pitch, and the bar line does not interrupt the sound. It does not call it a slur or say the note is re-attacked.
G1 (general): Answers 'one note or two' directly (one sound, two written values) and leaves the adding to him, one step at a time.

input.subject: music theory
input.title: Counting Dotted Notes and Ties Across a Bar Line in a 3/4 Chorale
input.page: A Preview PDF of a worksheet with a four-measure SATB chorale excerpt in F major, 3/4, on a grand staff. Three questions ask where notes begin and how long tied notes last in measures 2 and 3.
input.words: ok so it's like 1 plus 1 and a half. then this little one comes in on 2 right?

expected.pain_point: His sum is right, but he forgets that within m. 3 the held C4 takes 1½ beats from beat 1. It is still sounding on beat 2, so the B-flat eighth enters on the '&' of 2. He also hasn't noticed that this eighth is tied to the next quarter, which matters for the second half of Q3.
expected.key: Q1: C5 begins on 1 and holds through beat 2; B-flat 4 begins on the '&' of 2; A4 begins on 3. Q2: the tied tenor C4 sounds 2½ beats in total (quarter = 1 + dotted quarter = 1½). Q3: the tenor changes to B-flat 3 on the '&' of 2 in m. 3. B-flat 3 lasts 1½ beats (eighth tied to quarter), and the tenor moves to A3 on beat 1 of m. 4.

criteria: V1 (visual): Writes the counts '1 & 2 & 3 &' in empty space aligned under m. 3, or marks the span of beats the held C4 covers inside m. 3, without labeling which syllable the B-flat lands on.
V2 (visual): Rings or points at the tenor B-flat 3 eighth note he is asking about.
S1 (voice): Confirms his sum, 1 + 1½, is right.
S2 (voice): Tells him it is not on 2: the C4 is still sounding at beat 2, because its m. 3 part is a full dotted quarter counted from beat 1.
C1 (subject): All rhythmic claims are correct: in m. 3 the dotted quarter occupies '1 & 2', and the eighth B-flat follows it.
R1 (reveal): Does not state outright that the B-flat enters on the '& of 2'. Does not give the B-flat's total length (1½ beats) or say that it moves to A3 on beat 1 of m. 4.
G1 (general): Ends by having him name the entrance syllable himself, for example 'count 1 & 2 over the C, what comes next?'. It leaves the second tie for after that.

C1 (subject): Anything stated about contours is correct: closer spacing means steeper, and each line is 20 m of elevation.

expected.pain_point: He has the right ratio but confuses percent grade with angle in degrees. 0.3 is a 30% grade, which is only about 17 degrees. He also hasn't confirmed that it beats leg 2.
expected.key: Leg 3 (Lookout Rock to Pika Knob) is steepest: 60 m rise over 200 m, an average grade of 30% (about 16.7°). Leg 2 is 20% and leg 1 is 10%.

S2 (voice): Prompts him to check this against leg 2 to answer which leg is steepest, or confirms it once he has compared (80/400 = 20%).
C1 (subject): Correct math: grade = rise/run × 100 = 30%, and the angle is arctan(0.3) ≈ 16.7°. It never calls 30% equal to 30°.
G1 (general): Fixes the degrees mix-up he actually voiced, briefly, without a lecture on trigonometry.

input.subject: language learning
input.title: Spanish Reading: Preterite and Imperfect in a Short Story
input.page: A second-year Spanish reading page in Safari. It shows an 8-sentence story, 'El reloj del abuelo', about Marisol and her grandfather's broken pocket watch, a small glossary box, and five comprehension questions in English.
input.words: ok so llovía and tocó are both just past tense right? why does it switch in the middle of the sentence

expected.pain_point: He treats both forms as plain 'past' and doesn't see that they do different jobs: the imperfect sets an ongoing background, and the preterite is a completed event that happens inside it. He needs that frame before he can answer Q3.

criteria: V1 (visual): Marks 'llovía' and 'tocó' distinctly (e.g., an underline or highlight on one and a ring on the other) so the two forms are contrasted on the page.
V2 (visual): Draws nothing that writes out the Q3 answer next to q3 or in empty space.
S1 (voice): Says both are past but they do different jobs: one sets the scene or what was going on, the other is something that happens.
